newsitem.title: USA: Sallie Mae says $2.10 oper EPS sustainable.
newsitem.headline: Sallie Mae says $2.10 oper EPS sustainable.

text.p: Denise McGlone, chief financial officer of Student Loan Marketing Association (Sallie Mae) said Friday that the $2.10 in operating earnings per share recorded for the second quarter of 1997 can be achieved in the third and fourth quarters.
"We expect to sustain that for the rest of the year," McGlone said in a telephone interview from Washington.

Earlier, Sallie Mae reported net income of $2.20 per share for the second quarter of 1997, versus $1.79 a year ago. Core earnings, which adjust for the positive effect of a low interest rate environment, were $2.10 per share versus $1.63.
McGlone said the 29 percent year-over-year increase in operating earnings per share "reflect the power of the strategy that this management team has put in place."

The Sallie Mae management is asking shareholders to approve a slate or candidates for the board of directors and a plan to privatize the government-sponsored stockholder-owned company. An opposition group, the Committee to Restore Value (CRV), is running a rival slate. The CRV also seeks privatization but favors a business plan that would have Sallie Mae originate student loans intead of purchasing loans from banks.

Sallie Mae said in its earnings release that it purchased $2.1 billion of student loans in the second quarter. It said an additional $1.1 billion in purchases and future purchase commitments were postponed by sellers following statements by the CRV that it would begin origination of student loans if it gained control of the company.
The Sallie Mae management has argued that banks would back away from dealing with Sallie Mae if they believed it would be a competitor to their own lending programs.
"We would have had an exceptional quarter except for the damage created by the debate," McGlone said.
McGlone said of the $1.1 billion in postponed business, $250 million represented purchases on the "spot market." The remainder represented forward purchase commitments.
She said the main impact of the postponements was on "future earnings growth potential" and not current results.

McGlone said some banks have asked that contracts include clauses that Sallie Mae will not become a competitor. She said Sallie Mae has not agreed to that condition because "we don't want to box ourselves in."
"We're hoping that July 31 we win this battle," she added. The shareholder vote is set for that date.
Overall, McGlone said, Salle Mae is "hitting on all cylinders" of its business plan.

She noted that operating costs as a percentage of managed loans were 102 basis points in the second quarter, down from 111 basis points a year ago. "Our intention is to take that number from the low 100's to the low 80's." She said that could be achieved if the portfolio grew while costs were kept steady.
She said Sallie Mae is increasing its market share in the student loan business while that of the U.S. government, which has become a direct lender over the last several years, is declining.
